content: Respirators function in two primary ways to protect users. The first method involves removing contaminants from the air. This category includes particulate respirators, which filter out airborne particles, and gas masks, which filter out chemicals and gases. The second method involves supplying clean, breathable air from an external source. Examples of respirators in this category include airline respirators, which use compressed air from a remote source, and self-contained breathing apparatuses (SCBAs), which have their own air supply. Respirators should only be used when engineering control systems, such as proper ventilation or contaminant scrubbing, are not feasible or are insufficient. Engineering controls are the preferred method for reducing worker exposure to hazardous substances. The National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health (NIOSH) approves respirators in accordance with 42 Code of Federal Regulations Part 84 (42 CFR 84) and provides guidance for their use in occupational settings. Respirator standards are developed in collaboration with government and industry partners. NIOSH provides a trusted source of information on respiratory protection. This includes verifying NIOSH-approved respirators and offering resources on topics such as respirator selection and performance. The NIOSH Certified Equipment List (CEL) is the official database of all NIOSH-approved respirators. For concerns about respirators, individuals can contact the National Personal Protective Technology Laboratory (NPPTL) at PPEConcerns@cdc.gov. NIOSH has published several documents to address respiratory protection in various contexts: 1. Preparedness through Daily Practice: The Myths of Respiratory Protection in Healthcare (2016) This publication dispels common myths about respiratory protection and emphasizes the responsibilities of respiratory protection program administrators. It also educates healthcare workers on the proper use of respirators to prepare for public health emergencies and ensure daily safety. 2. Filtering Out Confusion: User Seal Check (2018) OSHA requires an annual fit test for respirators that form a tight seal on the face. After determining the best respirator model and size through fit testing, users must perform a seal check each time the respirator is worn to ensure an adequate seal. 3. Filtering Out Confusion: Fit Testing (2018) OSHA mandates annual fit testing to confirm that tight-fitting respirators provide the expected level of protection by minimizing contaminant leakage. This publication answers frequently asked questions about fit testing. 4. Filtering Out Confusion: Respirator Reuse and Extended Use (2018) Filtering facepiece respirators (FFRs) are typically disposable, but due to cost and supply considerations, there is interest in reusing or extending the use of undamaged and clean NIOSH-approved FFRs. This document addresses common questions about these practices. 5. A Guide to Atmosphere-Supplying Respirators (2019) Atmosphere-supplying respirators provide clean air from an independent source, protecting users from airborne contaminants and oxygen-deficient environments. Types include supplied-air respirators (SARs), SCBAs, and combination SAR/SCBA systems. 6. A Guide to Air-Purifying Respirators (2018) Air-purifying respirators (APRs) remove contaminants such as gases, vapors, and aerosols from the air using filters, cartridges, or canisters. These respirators do not supply oxygen and are unsuitable for oxygen-deficient or immediately dangerous to life or health (IDLH) environments. 7. Respirator Awareness: Your Health May Depend On It (2013) This publication highlights the risk of airborne transmission of infectious diseases in healthcare settings. It emphasizes that exposure risks extend beyond direct patient care to other workers, such as those involved in cleaning, food delivery, and maintenance. 8. NIOSH Respirator Selection Logic (2004) This document provides guidance for selecting respirators based on updated regulations and NIOSH policies. 9. NIOSH Pocket Guide to Chemical Hazards This guide offers industrial hygiene information on various chemicals and provides respirator recommendations based on exposure concentrations. NIOSH also provides resources such as a list of NIOSH-approved particulate filtering facepiece respirators (e.g., N95, P100) and information for manufacturers on applying for NIOSH approval. Additionally, NIOSH has developed videos and training materials on topics such as respirator certification, proper donning and doffing techniques, and the differences between respirators and surgical masks. OSHA has also produced videos covering topics such as respirator types, fit testing, maintenance, medical evaluations, and the importance of NIOSH certification. These resources aim to enhance understanding and compliance with respiratory protection standards.
